entities.name: Li Ching-Yuen
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Li Ching-Yuen, or Li Ching-Yun, stands as a captivating figure in the annals of longevity folklore, a Chinese herbalist, martial artist, and tactical advisor whose supposed extreme age—variously reported as 197, 256, or even 150 years—transcended mere human lifespan to become a cultural phenomenon. Though born in an unknown year, his death on May 6, 1933, in Chongqing, China, marked the end of a life shrouded in myth, influencing perceptions of human potential and traditional Chinese practices from the late Qing Dynasty through the early Republican Era. His significance lies not in verified historical events, but in his enduring role as an emblem of extraordinary health, spiritual discipline, and the pursuit of immortality, resonating deeply within Chinese cultural narratives and beyond.

Accounts of Li Ching-Yuen's life, largely unverified by modern historians, describe him as having begun his herbalist career at the age of ten, collecting herbs in the mountains of Sichuan and honing his knowledge of traditional Chinese medicine and martial arts. He reputedly traveled extensively, mastering various forms of Qigong and dietary practices believed to promote longevity. One widely cited anecdote claims that in 1927, General Yang Sen, a warlord of Sichuan, invited Li to his residence, where he was photographed and interviewed, allegedly confirming his advanced age. These interactions, though lacking rigorous corroboration, solidified his legend, portraying him as a living embodiment of ancient wisdom and physical mastery.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Li Ching-Yuen's story, regardless of its factual basis, profoundly influenced cultural perceptions of human longevity and the efficacy of traditional Chinese health practices, inspiring global interest in Qigong and herbalism. His legend continues to ripple through popular culture as a testament to the enduring human desire for extended life.
